questions.stem: An 85 kg man sustains partial and full thickness burns to 30% of his total body surface area. He is brought to hospital 2 hours after the injury.
questions.lead: According to the Parkland formula, how much crystalloid should he receive in the first 8 hours after injury, and over what remaining period?
options: 5100 mL over the next 8 hours from now
10 200 mL over the 6 hours from now
2550 mL over the next 8 hours from now
5100 mL over the 6 hours from now
2550 mL over the 6 hours from now
questions.explanation: Parkland is 4 mL × kg × %TBSA over 24 hours = 4 × 85 × 30 = 10 200 mL total, with half (5100 mL) in the first 8 hours and the remainder over the following 16. The second half of the rule is the one that catches people: the clock runs from the time of injury, not from arrival, so with 2 hours already elapsed the 5100 mL must go in over the remaining 6 hours, at a correspondingly faster rate. Using 2 mL/kg/%TBSA halves the total and under-resuscitates.
questions.point: Parkland is 4 mL/kg/%TBSA over 24 h, half in the first 8 hours measured from the time of injury, not from presentation.

questions.stem: An adult is in cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation. CPR is in progress in an Australian emergency department. Two shocks have been delivered and VF persists after the second rhythm check.
questions.lead: Under ANZCOR guidelines, which drugs should be given at this point?
options: Neither — both are given after the third shock
Adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg
Adrenaline 1 mg and lignocaine 100 mg, with amiodarone contraindicated
Adrenaline 1 mg only, with amiodarone withheld until after the fourth shock
Amiodarone 300 mg only, with adrenaline withheld until after the third shock
questions.explanation: ANZCOR gives adrenaline 1 mg after the second shock in a shockable rhythm, and amiodarone 300 mg is also given after the second shock, with adrenaline then repeated every second cycle. This is a genuine regional difference worth holding: the UK Resuscitation Council and ERC give both after the third shock. Answering "third shock" is correct for a European paper and wrong for an Australian one — which guideline the question is written to is decided by where you are sitting the exam.
questions.point: ANZCOR: adrenaline and amiodarone both after the second shock in shockable arrest; UK/ERC gives them after the third.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash. He is agitated, RR 34, SpO₂ 88% on 15 L oxygen, BP 78/44, HR 132. The trachea is deviated to the left, there are absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the right, and the neck veins are distended.
questions.lead: What is the immediate next step?
options: Immediate finger or needle decompression of the right chest, then continue the primary survey
Intubation and positive pressure ventilation
Rapid infusion of 2 L crystalloid, then reassess
FAST scan to exclude intra-abdominal haemorrhage
Chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis before intervening
questions.explanation: This is a tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis treated before imaging. Immediate finger or needle decompression of the affected side, followed by a definitive intercostal catheter, and then the primary survey continues from where it stopped. Waiting for a chest X-ray is the classic fatal delay. Positive pressure ventilation before decompression will worsen the tension and can precipitate arrest. Distended neck veins with hypotension distinguish this from simple haemorrhagic shock, where the veins are flat.
questions.point: Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically and decompressed immediately — never delayed for imaging, never ventilated first.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has 4 months of worsening back and rib pain. Bloods: Hb 92 g/L normochromic normocytic, calcium 2.92 mmol/L, creatinine 168 µmol/L, ALP 92 U/L (30–110), ESR 88 mm/h. Skeletal survey shows well-defined lytic lesions in the skull.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Osteoporosis with vertebral fractures
Multiple myeloma
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Metastatic prostate carcinoma
Paget disease of bone
questions.explanation: CRAB — hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions — with a very high ESR and lytic skull lesions is multiple myeloma. The discriminator from Paget disease is the biochemistry: Paget gives a markedly raised ALP with normal calcium, and sclerotic, thickened bone rather than punched-out lysis. Here ALP is normal and calcium is high — the exact reverse. Prostate metastases are characteristically sclerotic, and primary hyperparathyroidism would not produce this degree of anaemia and ESR elevation.
questions.point: Myeloma: high calcium with normal ALP and lytic lesions. Paget: very high ALP with normal calcium and sclerotic bone.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man has noticed a painless firm swelling in the left testis. Ultrasound confirms a 3 cm solid, hypoechoic intratesticular mass with increased vascularity. AFP and beta-hCG are pending.
questions.lead: How should the diagnosis be established?
options: Open trans-scrotal excisional biopsy
PET scan followed by targeted biopsy
Observation with repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks
Trans-scrotal needle biopsy
Radical inguinal orchidectomy
questions.explanation: A solid intratesticular mass is testicular cancer until proven otherwise, and the diagnosis is made by radical inguinal orchidectomy — which is simultaneously the diagnostic and the primary therapeutic procedure. Any trans-scrotal approach is contraindicated: the testis drains via the spermatic cord to the para-aortic nodes (following its embryological origin), and breaching the scrotum seeds the inguinal nodes, creating a metastatic route that would not otherwise exist and altering staging and radiotherapy fields. The same anatomy is why staging is by CT abdomen.
questions.point: Testicular cancer is diagnosed by radical inguinal orchidectomy — never trans-scrotal biopsy, which seeds inguinal nodes outside the para-aortic drainage.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a gastric ulcer found at endoscopy, biopsied as benign with Helicobacter pylori present. He completes eradication therapy and a urea breath test 6 weeks later is negative. He remains asymptomatic.
options: Lifelong proton pump inhibitor without endoscopic follow-up
No further endoscopic follow-up, as eradication is confirmed and he is asymptomatic
Repeat gastroscopy with biopsy to confirm ulcer healing
Annual gastroscopy for 5 years
CT abdomen to complete staging
questions.explanation: Gastric ulcers are re-scoped and re-biopsied to confirm healing, because an ulcerated gastric carcinoma can look benign and the initial biopsies can sample the wrong area. Neither symptom resolution nor confirmed eradication says anything about the mucosa, which is precisely why both are in the stem. Duodenal ulcers do not need this — they essentially never harbour malignancy, and a negative breath test closes the loop. That asymmetry is the point being tested.
questions.point: Gastric ulcers need repeat endoscopy and biopsy to exclude malignancy; duodenal ulcers do not.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man has abnormal liver tests on a routine check. AST 142 U/L, ALT 61 U/L, GGT 288 U/L, ALP 118 U/L (30–110), bilirubin 22 µmol/L, MCV 103 fL, platelets 134 × 10⁹/L, INR 1.1, albumin 38 g/L.
options: Acute viral hepatitis — request hepatitis serology as the priority
Normal synthetic function excludes significant chronic liver disease
A cholestatic picture — arrange urgent biliary imaging for obstruction
An alcohol-related hepatocellular pattern, with the platelet count raising concern for portal hypertension
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, given the modest transaminase elevation
questions.explanation: AST:ALT above 2 (142/61 = 2.3) with a raised GGT and macrocytosis is the alcohol signature; NAFLD characteristically shows ALT above AST. The pattern is hepatocellular, not cholestatic — the ALP is only marginally raised and bilirubin is near normal, so obstruction is not the story. Thrombocytopenia is the finding not to skip past: it suggests hypersplenism from portal hypertension and therefore established cirrhosis. Normal INR and albumin do not exclude cirrhosis — synthetic function is preserved until decompensation, so a normal set is not reassurance.
questions.point: AST:ALT above 2 with high GGT and macrocytosis is alcohol; low platelets suggest portal hypertension even when INR and albumin are normal.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer has distressing breathlessness at rest. She is on maximal treatment of the underlying disease. SpO₂ is 95% on room air, respiratory rate 26. She is opioid-naive.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate treatment for the breathlessness?
options: High-flow oxygen therapy
Regular nebulised salbutamol
Low-dose oral morphine
A benzodiazepine as first-line
Reassurance alone, as her oxygen saturation is normal
questions.explanation: Low-dose opioid is first-line for refractory breathlessness in advanced disease, and works independently of oxygen saturation — it reduces the central perception of breathlessness rather than correcting hypoxia. A normal SpO₂ is not a reason to withhold treatment, and oxygen confers no benefit in a non-hypoxaemic patient. Benzodiazepines are second-line, useful where anxiety is a major component, but not the starting point. Note that in an opioid-naive patient this means small doses with careful titration, not the doses used for pain.
questions.point: Refractory breathlessness in advanced disease is treated with low-dose morphine regardless of oxygen saturation; oxygen does not help the non-hypoxaemic.

questions.stem: A patient is being assessed preoperatively. On mouth opening with tongue protrusion, the soft palate and the base of the uvula are visible, but neither the uvular tip nor the tonsillar pillars can be seen.
questions.lead: What is the Mallampati class, and what does it predict?
options: Class IV — potentially difficult intubation
Class III — predicts difficult bag-mask ventilation but not intubation
Class I — no anticipated difficulty
Class II — intubation likely to be straightforward
Class III — potentially difficult intubation
questions.explanation: Mallampati III is soft palate and base of uvula only, and predicts potentially difficult intubation. The classes run: I soft palate, fauces, uvula and pillars; II soft palate, fauces and uvula; III soft palate and uvular base; IV hard palate only — no soft palate visible at all. Since some soft palate is visible here, class IV is excluded. Mallampati is only one component of airway assessment and is a weak predictor alone — it is combined with thyromental distance, mouth opening, neck extension and jaw protrusion.
questions.point: Mallampati III is soft palate plus uvular base; class IV shows hard palate only.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer has a malignant small bowel obstruction. She has colicky abdominal pain and vomiting. She is not a surgical candidate and is being managed medically for symptom control.
options: Metoclopramide
Ondansetron
Cyclizine
Levomepromazine
Haloperidol
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide is a prokinetic, and increasing peristalsis against a mechanical obstruction worsens colic and risks perforation — it is contraindicated where obstruction is complete or colic is prominent. The appropriate agents act centrally without stimulating motility: haloperidol (chemoreceptor trigger zone), cyclizine (antihistaminergic, useful in bowel obstruction), or levomepromazine as a broad-spectrum option. Hyoscine butylbromide is added as an antispasmodic and antisecretory agent, with octreotide for high-volume vomiting.
questions.point: Metoclopramide is avoided in bowel obstruction — prokinesis against a mechanical block worsens colic.
